newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - German economic blues benefit Bunds.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - German economic blues benefit Bunds.

text.p: Bunds will offer good opportunities to investors and are likely to outperform U.S. Treasuries in the coming weeks as weakness in the German economy continues, analysts said on Thursday.
Earlier, Germany released data showing unemployment had risen to 4.66 million in January from 4.1 million in December, emphasising this weakness.
"The economy is still very much on its knees with the weak orders numbers yesterday and the shockingly large rise in unemployment," said Huw Roberts, at NatWest Capital Markets.

"Germany has already got a very easy monetary policy stance and it doesn't appear to be paying any dividends at the moment. It's got to beg the question, Do they need to ease monetary policy further?" said Roberts, a European bond strategist here.
Analysts said the outlook for the Bund market was particularly positive against a backdop of continued solid growth in the U.S.
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) kept U.S. monetary policy unchanged after its meeting earlier this week -- although many analysts believe a rate hike is just a matter of time.
Michael Lewis, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London, said growth in the U.S. was better than in Germany, and the focus will now be on the March FOMC meeting.
This was likely to lead to Bunds outperforming U.S. Treasuries, and he said DMG's spread target continued to be 100 basis points.
"We're still looking for high U.S. yields, so in terms of Bunds we are continuing to see upward potential," he said.
The 10-year T-note/Bund spread is currently showing an 88 basis point premium in U.S. yields.

Meanwhile the Bundesbank decided on Thursday to keep its repo rate unchanged at a fixed 3.0 percent for the next two securities repurchase tenders. The announcement was made after the regular meeting of the Bundesbank on Thursday.
Julian Jessop, European economist at Nikko Europe in London, said the unemployment figures did not directly influence the Bundesbank's monetary policy.
"The Bundesbank has always regarded unemployment as a structural problem which can't be solved by monetary policy," he said. "But, as part of the bigger picture they are important."
The high level of unemployment would suppress business and consumer confidence, thus ultimately playing a part in any decision on interest rates, he said.
Lewis said further out, the unemployment data would not be completely positive for Bunds as it could lead to increased government spending and affect the budget deficit.
"That will lead to continued weak growth and the chances that the three percent (Maastricht) target will not be reached," he said. "This period is going to be a bit of an aberration."
He said the economy would remain weak in the first quarter, which would be supportive to German bonds, but he saw some modest growth coming through after that.
"So it is maybe a bit of an exaggerated picture for Germany right now," Lewis said.
Roberts also expected Germany to outperform both against the European high yielders and against the U.S., where he saw the spread likely to widen through 100 basis points.

"The economic situation does suggest the backdrop for Bunds is very benign," he said. "If we do get any sell-offs, for example tommorrow on the U.S. payrolls, it is just a better buying opportunity. There is nothing to really threaten the Bund market."
